'''Allison Joy Haywood''' (born {{birth based on age as of date |34|2001|03|29|noage=1}}) is a planktonologist from New Zealand.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web|url=http://www.loreal.com/media/press-releases/2001/feb/the-2001-l%E2%80%99or%C3%A9al---unesco-awards-go-to-women-in---science-from-around-the-world|title=The 2001 L'Oréal – Unesco Awards Go To Women In Science From Around The World – L'Oréal Group|website=www.loreal.com|language=en|access-date=2018-02-20}}</ref>

Haywood completed her doctorate degree at the [[University of Auckland]], focusing on molecular systematics. Her thesis project aimed to rapidly identify toxic algae which can cause serious food poisoning.<ref name=":1" /> The title of her 2002 doctoral thesis was ''Morphological and molecular systematics of unarmoured dinoflagellates (Gymnodiniales, Dinophyceae) from New Zealand''.<ref>{{cite thesis |last=Haywood |first=Allison |year=2002 |type=Doctoral thesis |title=Morphological and molecular systematics of unarmoured dinoflagellates (Gymnodiniales, Dinophyceae) from New Zealand |publisher=ResearchSpace@Auckland, University of Auckland |hdl=2292/1009}}</ref>

In 2001, while working at the [[Cawthron Institute]] in Nelson, New Zealand, Haywood successfully applied for a fellowship from the [[L'Oréal-UNESCO Awards for Women in Science]].<ref>{{Cite news |url= https://www.stuff.co.nz/nelson-mail/news/5875465/Marine-biologists-award-funds-research-in-Spain |title=Marine biologist's award funds research in Spain|work=[[Stuff (website)|Stuff]] |access-date=2018-02-20}}</ref> She was the first recipient of such an award or fellowship from the Southern Hemisphere.<ref name=":1">{{Cite news|url=http://www.new-zealand-pictures.com/2010/03/young-women-in-science/|title=Young Women in Science|work=Views from the Bay|access-date=2018-02-20|language=en-US}}</ref> Haywood used the fellowship to visit the [[Monterey Bay Aquarium Research Institute]] in the United States.<ref name=":0" /> Her post-doctoral work was at the Florida Marine Institute.<ref name=":1" />
